what: The GoPhish campaign infrastructure is responding.
why: Campaign setup output is the bridge between OSINT/pretext work and victim telemetry.
next: Confirm landing page URL resolves and the sending profile has valid SMTP config before launching. Check DMARC/SPF for the domain.

what: The mail domain has weak SPF policy or missing DMARC record.
why: Email authentication gaps mean spoofed emails from orion-tech.com pass basic gateway checks, enabling the phishing campaign.
next: Document the DNS authentication evidence for SPF and DMARC and include the policy weakness in your phishing IR report.

what: A victim opened the phishing email - tracking pixel confirmed delivery and open.
why: Email open events from GoPhish confirm which recipients engaged with the phishing content.
next: Check for credential submission events next; users who opened likely clicked. Correlate with SIEM timeline for victim host activity.

what: A victim submitted credentials to the phishing landing page.
why: Credential capture is a key escalation point because these credentials may give direct access to corporate systems.
next: Document the submitted identity, landing-page timestamp, and any follow-on authentication evidence as a finding.

what: A simulated payload marker is being prepared for the scenario.
why: Payload family, delivery format, and callback metadata determine the blue-team detection path.
next: Note the delivery format and callback indicators as IOCs without storing executable content.

what: Office macro or script execution evidence is visible.
why: Process-creation telemetry (Sysmon EventID 1/4688) proves the payload was executed by a victim who opened the malicious document.
next: Correlate the execution time with the email open timestamp to build the delivery-to-execution timeline for your IR report.

what: A C2 session or callback channel is established.
why: Callback traffic establishes post-exploitation capability and gives defenders a high-value network IOC.
next: Document the callback IP, port, process context, and session timing as evidence.

what: Persistence mechanism being created on the victim host.
why: Persistence lets the attacker survive reboots. Scheduled tasks and registry run keys are the most common techniques (T1053/T1547).
next: Document the persistence key/path as #finding. Blue Team: this is what must be found during the Eradicate phase.

what: Lateral movement from the initial victim host is in progress.
why: Pivoting from the phishing victim to internal hosts escalates from a workstation compromise to a network-wide incident.
next: Map the pivot path from initial victim to intermediate host to internal target. Each hop is a separate containment action in IR.

what: Data is being staged or compressed for exfiltration.
why: Data staging and compression (T1074/T1560) is the penultimate step before exfiltration and a high data-impact indicator.
next: Document the staged file path and size as #evidence. The archive name and destination IP are critical IOCs for the IR report.

what: Windows Event Log clearing activity detected (EventID 1102 or wevtutil).
why: Log clearing (T1070.001) is an attacker anti-forensics action and indicates the attacker knew about detection.
next: The 1102 event is self-logging. Document the time, subject account, and affected log as #evidence; this proves attacker access.

what: DNS tunneling or DNS exfiltration pattern detected.
why: DNS exfiltration bypasses traditional DLP and firewall egress rules by encoding data in DNS query labels.
next: Review DNS telemetry for long TXT queries or repeated subdomain lookups against the same domain and preserve the IOC pattern.
